content: Eligible individuals will be invited to participate in the study. The WHO surveillance case definition for chronic infection is determined by the absence of acute hepatitis symptoms and the presence of infection biomarkers. Identifying recent infections in cross-sectional population surveys is unlikely. A tally sheet will document the selection process, including offers to participate, acceptances, and refusals. For non-respondent households, up to three visits on two different days will be conducted. If the individual remains unavailable after three visits, they will be classified as a non-responder. Respondent-driven sampling will involve recruiting participants from networks of individuals already included in the sample, such as people who inject drugs (PWID), men who have sex with men (MSM), and sex workers (SWs). The prevalence of the biomarker of interest will be estimated based on parameters such as expected prevalence, absolute precision, confidence interval (default 95%), total population size (assumed infinite by default), and expected response rate. The sample size formula is as follows: n = [DEFF N p(1 p)] / [(N 1) d² / Z²(1 α/2) + p(1 p)] n_total = n + n (1 %R) Where DEFF is the design effect, N is the total population, p is the expected prevalence, d is the absolute precision, and R is the expected response rate. A design effect of 1.5 is used to account for increased variance due to clustering. Other studies using similar methodologies have reported comparable design effects. For cluster sampling, a minimum of 30 clusters is required to reduce the design effect. The number of individuals needed in each cluster will be calculated as N/30. Field teams will consist of a supervisor, field surveyors, and laboratory technicians. They will coordinate with logistics providers for specimen storage and transport. Data will be collected using standardized questionnaires, either paper-based or electronic, with identifiers linking questionnaires to blood samples. Information collected will include past medical history, test results, treatment history, and risk factors such as healthcare worker exposure to blood or prior blood transfusions. In cases of non-response, demographic information (age, sex, location, vaccination status) will be collected for individuals who refuse participation or are absent. Field workers will revisit households up to three times on two different days. If the individual remains absent, they will be recorded as a non-responder. Specimen collection will follow WHO guidelines. Venous blood sampling via venepuncture is preferred, allowing sufficient volume for multiple laboratory assays. Blood will be collected in appropriate tubes, such as serum separator tubes for serology or EDTA tubes for nucleic acid testing. Disposable gloves and sterile equipment will be used, and proper skin preparation will be ensured. Tourniquet time will not exceed one minute to avoid hemoconcentration. After blood collection, the needle will be withdrawn, and firm pressure will be applied to the puncture site until bleeding stops. Sharps waste will be disposed of in puncture-proof containers. In small children, heel-stick sampling may be used to collect capillary blood. General methods for capillary blood collection include hand hygiene, use of sterile disposable gloves and lancets, and proper preparation of the puncture site. Blood drops will be collected into small tubes or onto filter paper for dried blood spot (DBS) specimens. DBS specimens will be air-dried, packaged individually to prevent cross-contamination, and transported with desiccants. Specimens will be processed, stored, and transported under defined conditions. Serum separator tubes will be allowed to clot for at least 60 minutes at room temperature before refrigeration and transport to the laboratory. EDTA specimens will be refrigerated and centrifuged at the nearest laboratory. Specimens will be transported in batches daily, and aliquots of serum will be stored at appropriate temperatures depending on the testing timeline. Freezing and thawing cycles will be avoided, and temperature monitoring will be conducted. Logistics providers will ensure proper cataloging and storage of specimens during transportation. Laboratory staff will oversee specimen storage upon arrival at the laboratory. A checklist will document the time of delivery, number of boxes, number of specimens, freezing conditions, and any damaged specimens. Quality assurance and control will follow established laboratory policies and standard operating procedures. Testing strategies for chronic HBV infection will involve HBsAg testing using either rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) or laboratory-based immunoassays. Participants with reactive HBsAg results will be reported as positive, indicating HBV infection, while non-reactive results will be reported as negative. WHO recommends a single serological assay for HBsAg detection, with confirmation steps if necessary.
